title.zh: 傑倫特與「燕隼」比武大會

region.en: Town of the sparrow-hawk tournament, South Wales (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南威爾士燕隼比武之城（象徵定位）

texts.period: Geraint the Son of Erbin, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Riding with Gwenhwyvar after the hunt, Geraint follows a knight, a lady and a dwarf who abuses the queen's maiden and beats the men who defend her; at the town he learns the lady's knight holds the sparrow-hawk by right of victory, and that the dwarf will throw off any man who claims the honour for a poor knight's wife. Geraint undertakes the honour for Enid, whom he finds fitting to it, overthrows the knight, and wins both the sparrow-hawk and the hand of Enid the golden.
summary.zh: 獵後隨格溫赫薇爾出遊的傑倫特，遇見騎士、淑女與矮人一行；矮人辱打王后的侍女及其護衛。至城中，他得知那位騎士憑連勝保有「燕隼」殊榮，而矮人專門羞辱為貧窮騎士之妻爭榮者。傑倫特為埃妮德出戰——他認定她當得起此榮——擊敗對手，贏得燕隼與金髮埃妮德之手。

sensitivity.note: Geraint (Erec in Chretien) is the Welsh Arthurian romance; the sparrow-hawk custom (the victor's right at the tournament) is a chivalric institution grafted onto native tale-stock; the insult to the queen's maiden drives the plot as transgression. Symbolic pin in South Wales.

passages.text: And when they came near to the knight and the lady, and the dwarf, the dwarf was a jester that laughed at the queen; and he came near the maiden that was behind the queen, and he smote her a blow with his whip, so that she was wounded by it... And the maiden cried out, and cried for help: "Hast thou seen, lord," said she, "the treatment that the dwarf gave me?" And the men that were near her said to her, "Go after the dwarf." And she went, and Geraint, and she caught the dwarf by the collar of his dress... and the dwarf drew his sword, and he dealt her a blow with it; and the maiden stood aside, and the blow reached the ear of her hood; and Geraint drew his sword... and they fought, and Geraint overthrew the dwarf, and took his horse from him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Geraint went to the town, and he asked a hoary-headed man, that was by the gate, what was the custom of the town: "The knight that is yonder," said he, "the lady that is with him, is his wife; and he keepeth the sparrow-hawk; and if any one will contend with him for it, he can win it by overcoming him in fair fight... And the dwarf will take the honour from him, because his wife is not of his rank." "Then will I contend for the sparrow-hawk for my wife," said Geraint... And Geraint overthrew the knight, and took his horse and his arms, and gave them to the hoary-headed man; and he took the sparrow-hawk, and bore it in his hand, and rode through the town to the place where Enid was, and he gave it to her, and he said, "This honour I have won for thee." And Enid rejoiced, and her father rejoiced with her, and Geraint took her to wife at Arthur's court.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.

title.en: Enid's Whisper and the Robbers of the Road
title.zh: 埃妮德的低語與路上的強盜

region.en: Roads of the March, Wales (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 威爾士邊境之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Geraint the Son of Erbin, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Grown idle in love, Geraint neglects the affairs of the kingdom until Arthur restores him to his own; Enid's whisper that his arms are rusted for lack of use he takes for faithlessness, and rides out commanding silence on pain of death. Yet on the road three bands of robbers come upon them one after another, and Enid's three warnings save him each time; her silence kept and broken, the journey of the rusted arms becomes the trial that restores the marriage.
summary.zh: 溺於愛情的傑倫特荒廢國政，直至亞瑟王令他復位；埃妮德低語「他的甲胄已因閒置而生鏽」，他誤以為妻子變心，遂令她保持緘默——違者死。然路上一連三夥強盜襲來，埃妮德三次示警救他；緘默的禁令與破除，使這趟「生鏽甲胄」之旅成為修復婚姻的試煉。

sensitivity.note: The silence-on-pain-of-death taboo of Geraint is the fixed jealous-husband device of the Erec story-type; the three robbers' bands are the staged trial-rhythm of romance roads. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And Geraint loved Enid, and loved her so entirely that he was glad to be alone with her in the chamber, and to make delight and conversation with her, and to leave the business of his kingdom and his subjects... And Enid was one morning in bed, and Geraint by her side, and she wept... "Alas, that I ever was born, that I have caused my lord's arms to rust for want of use!" And Geraint heard her words, and there came over him great wrath; and he rose up, and he took his arms and his horse, and he said, "Lady, I will go forth, and thou shalt go with me; and if thou speakest to me on the road, thy head shall be cut off."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.

passages.text: And as they went thus, they beheld three horsemen coming towards them, and Enid knew that they were three robbers, and she was afraid for Geraint, and she sighed... and Geraint turned his head, and saw that Enid was opening her lips to speak; and he threatened her, and she was silent... And the three robbers made upon him with their weapons; and Geraint slew them, every one of them. And they went on, and there came against them three more, and after them three again; and every time Enid could not forbear to give warning, and every time Geraint overcame them; and at last he saw that the warnings had saved him. And at the supper in the Earl's court, when the Earl would have her by force, Enid cried aloud for Geraint, and he rose from the table, and smote off the Earl's head, and laid his sword by her side, and said, "Thou art free; and none shall harm thee."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.

title.en: Kilhwch Seeks Olwen at Arthur's Gate
title.zh: 基爾赫在亞瑟門前求娶奧爾文

region.en: Arthur's palace at Kelliwic, Cornwall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 康沃爾凱利維克的亞瑟王宮（象徵定位）

texts.period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Culhwch — Kilhwch, son of Kilydd — is doomed by his stepmother to win no wife but Olwen, daughter of the giant Yspaddaden Penkawr, and blushing at a love he has never seen, he rides to Arthur to cut his hair: two silver-headed spears, gold-hilted sword, ivory horn, two white-breasted greyhounds with ruby collars bounding like sea-swallows, and an apple of gold at every corner of the purple cloth about him. The porter's laws and Arthur's renunciation of his own boons frame the greatest quest-catalogue of the corpus.
summary.zh: 庫爾赫（基利德之子基爾赫）被繼母施咒：除非娶巨人格雅斯帕達丹·彭考爾之女奧爾文，否則終身無妻。未曾謀面卻已然面紅心跳的他騎向亞瑟王求助：雙銀矛、金柄劍、象牙號角、紅寶石項圈的白胸靈緹如海燕般跳躍，紫袍四角各綴一枚百牛價值的金蘋果。守門者之法與亞瑟自縛的誓言，開啟了本語料庫最宏偉的探求清單。

sensitivity.note: The stepmother's love-spell doom (a destiny-wish said in anger) is the Welsh framing of the hostile-wish motif; the hair-cutting boon (Arthur as his cousin-godfather) parallels the haircut rite of Gaelic inauguration; the gate-laws catalogue is the fixed Arthurian-porter set-piece. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Then said she unto him, "I declare to thee, that it is thy destiny not to be suited with a wife until thou obtain Olwen, the daughter of Yspaddaden Penkawr." And the youth blushed, and the love of the maiden diffused itself through all his frame, although he had never seen her... And the youth pricked forth upon a steed with head dappled grey, of four winters old, firm of limb, with shell-formed hoofs, having a bridle of linked gold on his head... And in the youth's hand were two spears of silver, sharp, well-tempered, headed with steel, three ells in length, of an edge to wound the wind, and cause blood to flow, and swifter than the fall of the dewdrop from the blade of reed-grass upon the earth when the dew of June is at the heaviest. A gold-hilted sword was upon his thigh... his war-horn was of ivory. Before him were two brindled white-breasted greyhounds, having strong collars of rubies about their necks... and like two sea-swallows sported around him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

passages.text: Said the youth, "I came not here to consume meat and drink; but if I obtain the boon that I seek, I will requite it thee, and extol thee; and if I have it not, I will bear forth thy dispraise to the four quarters of the world, as far as thy renown has extended." Then said Arthur, "Since thou wilt not remain here, chieftain, thou shalt receive the boon whatsoever thy tongue may name, as far as the wind dries, and the rain moistens, and the sun revolves, and the sea encircles, and the earth extends; save only my ship; and my mantle; and Caledvwlch, my sword; and Rhongomyant, my lance; and Wynebgwrthucher, my shield; and Carnwenhau, my dagger; and Gwenhwyvar, my wife. By the truth of Heaven, thou shalt have it cheerfully, name what thou wilt." "I would that thou bless my hair." "That shall be granted thee."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

title.zh: 奧爾文的花朵與彭考爾的巨堡

region.zh: 彭考爾巨人城堡（象徵定位）

texts.period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Where Olwen walked, four white trefoils sprang up behind her — wherefore she was called Olwen, she of the white track — and the maiden opened the gate and came forth, more glorious than any maiden in the world, with a robe of flame-coloured silk, a ruby torc, and hair yellower than the flower of the broom, whiter than the foam of the wave, redder than the red heather. Her father's fort has nine gates; each is guarded, and every gate Kilhwch's men break in turn until the giant's long contest of impossible tasks begins.
summary.zh: 奧爾文行走之處，身後便生出四葉白花——故名「白足者奧爾文」。少女推開堡門而出：火焰色絲袍、紅寶石頸環；秀髮比金雀花更黃、比浪花更白、比赤石楠更紅，世間無雙。其父城堡有九重門，門門有守衛；基爾赫的部下一一破門而入，巨人那場「不可能任務」的漫長角力由此展開。

sensitivity.note: Olwen's flower-footsteps are the fixed eponym-aetiology of the tale (white track) and one of the great nature-images of Welsh myth; the nine-gate fort with a warder at each is the tower-of-tests pattern. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And they knew that it was Olwen that had opened the gate, and that she was coming forth; for where she walked, four white trefoils sprang up behind her; wherefore she was called Olwen, from the trefoils that sprang up in her track. And the maiden came forth, and she was arrayed in a robe of flame-coloured silk, and about her neck was a collar of rubies, with emeralds and pearls. And her hair was yellower than the flower of the broom, and whiter than the foam of the wave, and fairer than any sight that men had ever seen; and her skin was whiter than the snow, and her cheeks redder than the red heather.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Kilhwch saluted her: "Maiden, I love thee, nor can I live without thee." "I know thee not," said Olwen, "neither do I know thy name." "Kilhwch, son of Kilydd, am I; and my mother Goleuddydd, daughter of the prince Anlawdd..." "I will go and ask my father," said Olwen... And the fort had nine gates, and each of them had a warder; and every one of the gates was broken by Kilhwch's men; and the hall was broken through, and the huge warrior Yspaddaden was brought forth... "I will consult the virgin Olwen, and if she will have thee, thou shalt have her; but come hither again with the troop and see what I shall say." And Kilhwch's men broke the gates a second time, and a third time, until at the last the giant's wedding-feast and the hunts of the impossible boar were promised for the bride.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

title.zh: 追獵特爾赫·特魯伊斯的野豬

region.zh: 自德費德至康沃爾，威爾士

texts.period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Between the ears of the monstrous boar Twrch Trwyth lie the comb and the scissors Yspaddaden demands for his daughter's hair — a king transformed by God's curse into a swine with seven pigs at his back, who has slain many of Arthur's men. The hunt runs through all Wales: the boar lands at Amruth, crosses Severn, ravages Dyfed and Gower, is harried by Arthur himself, and at the last Grugyn and his boars are driven to the sea; the comb and shears are taken and the son of the king loses seven of his men for every gate of the fortress.
summary.zh: 巨野豬特爾赫·特魯伊斯雙耳之間藏著彭考爾為女兒梳髮所需的梳與剪——他本是受神詛化為豬形的國王，身後跟著七隻小豬，已殺亞瑟部眾多人。獵事縱貫全威爾士：登陸阿姆魯斯，橫渡塞文河，肆虐德費德與高爾，亞瑟王親自追擊，最終格魯金與豬群被逐入海。梳剪既得，城堡每道門的代價都是七條人命。

sensitivity.note: The transformed-king boar (Twrch Trwyth was a king turned to swine for sin, with seven pigs — the seven sons) is one of the finest Celtic shape-curse narratives; the comb-and-scissors prize parallels the Fenian comb-and-shears (Diarmuid's) — noted for cross-tradition echo. Pin follows the hunt's route.

passages.text: "It will not be easy for thee to obtain that which thou seekest," said Yspaddaden, "until thou get the comb and the scissors that are between the two ears of Twrch Trwyth... He is a king, and for his wickedness God transformed him into a swine, and he has seven pigs with him, and he will slay many of thy men." And Arthur made for him the muster of the whole island of Britain, and they set forth, and went as far as Dyfed... And Twrch Trwyth came and went to Severn, and the host came after him, and he crossed the Severn... and there was a great struggle between the host and the boar, and many men were slain of the one and of the other; and the boar went into Gower, and there the chase came upon him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

passages.text: And the hunt went on through the length of the land: Grugyn Silver-bristles, that was like a wing of wild birds, made his way through Din Tywi with his boars, and from Din Tywi to Din Emrys; and the men of Dyfed and the men of Gower could not prevail against him... And there was a great struggle between the host and the boar, and many men were slain of the one and of the other; and the boar went into Gower, and there the chase came upon him; and at the last Grugyn and his boars were driven into the sea, and the comb and the shears were taken from between the ears of Twrch Trwyth, and borne to Yspaddaden for the hair of Olwen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

title.en: Mabon son of Modron Freed from the Walls of Gloucester
title.zh: 莫德隆之子馬邦自格洛斯特獄中獲釋

region.zh: 不列顛格洛斯特（卡厄爾·洛伊）

texts.period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: One of Yspaddaden's boons is Mabon son of Modron, taken from his mother at three nights old and held where no man ever set him free. The oldest animals are asked in turn — the Blackbird of Cilgwri, the Stag of Rhedynfre, the Owl of Cwm Cawlwyd, the Eagle of Gwernabwy, and last the Salmon of Llyn Llyw — and the salmon carries Cai and Gwrhyr under the walls of Gloucester to the captive, who breaks the prison with his own strength, aided by the fighting of Arthur's host and the beasts of the hunt.
summary.zh: 彭考爾的條件之一是釋放「莫德隆之子馬邦」——出生三夜即被擄走，囚於無人曾令囚徒脫身之地。諸獸依次被問——基爾格里之黑鶇、雷丁弗雷之雄鹿、庫姆考爾維德之貓頭鷹、格威納布威之鷹——最終林利湖的鮭魚載著凱與格爾希爾潛入格洛斯特牆下；馬邦以自身神力破獄而出，亞瑟王的軍隊與獵獸協力相助。

sensitivity.note: The divine captive Mabon (maponos, the youth-god, son of Matrona/Modron) is attested in Romano-British cult; the chain of oldest animals (blackbird-stag-owl-eagle-salmon) is the classic cumulative-wisdom device, and the salmon-taxi under a prison wall parallels Finn's salmon of knowledge. Pin is the historical Gloucester.

passages.text: And they asked the Blackbird of Cilgwri, and he said, "When I first came here, there was a smith's anvil here, and I was then a young bird; and no work has been done on it save by my beak, and nothing is left of it but a nutmeg. And the oak has grown from a withered stub." And they asked the Stag of Rhedynfre... And they asked the Owl of Cwm Cawlwyd... And they asked the Eagle of Gwernabwy... "And I went to the rock of Llech Wen, and there I heard of Mabon son of Modron; and it was the Salmon of Llyn Llyw that told me, for he has been longer than I."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Cai and Gwrhyr went upon the shoulders of the fishes, and they came to the wall of the prison of Mabon; and they heard one lamenting and crying out: "And what lamentation is that?" "It is Mabon, son of Modron, that is here imprisoned; and no imprisonment was ever so grievous as mine." And Cai and Gwrhyr came before Mabon, and told him that Kilhwch sought him for the bride of Olwen. And Mabon was released by the strength of his own hand and of Arthur's men; and he was brought before Kilhwch, and the giant's task was paid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.

title.en: Rhonabwy's Dream and the Game of Gwyddbwyll
title.zh: 羅納布威之夢與格威德布威爾棋局

region.zh: 波伊斯里夫·赫爾維格（象徵定位）

texts.period: The Dream of Rhonabwy, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Rhonabwy, a retainer of Madog ap Maredudd, sleeps three days and three nights on the yellow calf-skin of a wizard's house and dreams he is on the plain of Argyll: Arthur's vast host comes and goes, the Emperor wears a cape of purple and gold that shines like fire, Osla GylmaW plays gwyddbwyll with him while the battle is lost and won, and the dream's chronology — two days and a night — mocks the hour of a dreamer's sleep. The tale is the Mabinogion's most self-conscious satire of Arthurian memory.
summary.zh: 馬多格·阿普·馬雷杜德的侍從羅納布威在巫師屋中的黃牛皮上沉睡三日三夜，夢見自己身處阿蓋爾平原：亞瑟的大軍來去如潮，皇帝披著火光般輝耀的紫金披風；戰事成敗之際，奧斯拉正與他對弈格威德布威爾。夢中的時間——兩日一夜——嘲弄著做夢者片刻的沉睡。此篇是《馬比諾吉安》中最自覺的亞瑟記憶諷刺。

sensitivity.note: The Dream of Rhonabwy is a late (c. 13th c.) literary dream-vision satirising the inflated Arthurian host and its heraldry; the game of gwyddbwyll during battle is the Welsh analogue of the Irish fidchell-with-battle motif (Midir's fidchell, Cuchulainn's). Pin symbolic in Powys.

passages.text: And Rhonabwy went into the house, and there was the calf's skin of a red yellow spread on the floor, and he lay down on it... And he slept three days and three nights. And in his sleep he beheld a vision: he was going over the plain of Argyll, and he saw before him a shoal of horses, and riders, and companies... And he beheld a knight coming towards him, sitting upon a horse of pure white, with a red-yellow cape about him, fringed with gold... And Rhonabwy asked who he was: "I am Iddawg, son of Mynyo, and I was the messenger between Arthur and Medrawd, at the battle of Camlan."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, The Dream of Rhonabwy; not verbatim.

passages.text: And they came towards the place where Arthur was, playing at gwyddbwyll with Osla GylmaW; and the board was of gold, and the men of silver... And Arthur said, "Rhonabwy, hast thou news?" And he beheld the men of the host going and coming, and knights and arms, and yellow capes of gold upon the horses... And the Emperor Arthur wore a cape of purple and of gold, and it shone like fire, and he had a sceptre in his hand, and a circle of gold about his head. And Arthur said to Iddawg, "Call thou to me all the men of my host, that they may see Rhonabwy." And when the game of gwyddbwyll was lost and won, the battle that was fought between the host of Arthur and the host of Medrawd was seen coming to the spot where the game was ended; and he who won the game had won the battle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, The Dream of Rhonabwy; not verbatim.

title.en: Math's Feet on a Maiden's Lap and Gilvaethwy's Punishment
title.zh: 數學王雙足倚於處女膝上與吉爾維斯威之懲罰

region.zh: 威爾士圭內斯卡厄爾·達斯爾

texts.period: Math the Son of Mathonwy, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Math son of Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd, cannot live but with his feet in the lap of a maiden, save when the land is at war; Goewin daughter of Pebin holds the office of foot-holder. Gwydion procures a war to draw Math out — a conjured fleet of pigs and shoes and shields, gifts that turn to toadstools by morning — and Gilvaethwy ravishes Goewin while the court is at Caer Dathyl. Math strikes with his wand: brother and brother become hind and stag, boar and sow, wolves for three years' terms, bearing young each year until the penance is paid.
summary.zh: 圭內斯之主馬松威之子馬，非戰時雙足必倚於處女膝上方能存活；佩賓之女格溫擔此職。吉威恩製造戰爭誘馬王離宮——以幻術變出豬群、鞋履與盾牌，晨光下盡成牛肝菌——而吉爾維斯威趁機玷污了格溫。馬以魔杖施刑：兄弟二人三年間輪為雌鹿與雄鹿、母豬與公豬、狼與狼，年年產幼，直到罪罰償清。

sensitivity.note: The foot-holder taboo (Math's feet in a maiden's lap) is the classic Welsh sacred-king infirmity motif, paralleled by Nuadu's arm in Irish tradition; the animal-transformation penance for rape is the fourth Branch's core justice-myth. The conjured war-gifts that become toadstools is Gwydion's signature magic. Pin is the named Caer Dathyl.

passages.text: Math the son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and Pryderi the son of Pwyll was lord over the one-and-twenty Cantrevs of the South; and Math has this property, that if men whisper together, in a tone how small soever, so that the wind can catch it, no sooner had the wind borne it to him than his mind becomes confused, and he can have no delight in anything but to lie with his two feet in the lap of a maiden, unless the pressure of illness prevents him. Now the maiden who was with him was Goewin, the daughter of Pebin, of Dol Bebin, and she was the fairest maiden of her time who was known in all Britain. And Math lay with his feet in her lap, so long as there was peace in the land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Gwydion procured that a fleet should be seen coming over the sea, and thirty ships in it, and the ships full of piss-glass... And there was with them every kind of arms and of horses; and Math went to the war, and his feet left the lap of the maiden. And Gilvaethwy the son of Don, and they that were with him, made an attack upon the maiden, and ravished her. And when Math came back, Goewin told him, and Math took his wand and struck Gilvaethwy, and changed him into a hind, and Gwydion into a stag, and he put them out from among men... And at the end of the third year he changed them into boars and swine, and at the end of three years more into wolves; and each year they brought forth young; and the young ones he took and baptized. And at the end of three years more he released them from that punishment, and changed them into their own shape.

title.en: Gronw's Dart and Lleu Standing on One Foot
title.zh: 格羅努之飛鏢與單足而立的勒烏

region.en: Gronw's hill of Bryn Kyvergyr, North Wales (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北威爾士布萊恩·基維吉爾山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Math the Son of Mathonwy, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Blodeuwedd's treachery asks Lleu the manner of his death, and the forbidden manner is told: by a river under a roofed cauldron, one foot on a cauldron and the other on a buck-goat, no weapon but a spear a year in the making and forged only on the Sabbath — and Gronw Pebyr rests on one knee on a hill and flings the poisoned dart. The wounded Lleu becomes an eagle in an oak, rotted flesh falling from him, until Gwydion finds him by the swine and restores him; and Lleu's own spear, cast with wrath, goes through Gronw and the stone he held before him, the stone that lies at Ardudwy still.
summary.zh: 布洛德威斯的背叛探知了勒烏的死法禁忌：屋中釜上、一足踏釜一足踏雄山羊、僅能以歷一年鍛成且只可在安息日打造的矛擊殺。格羅努·佩比爾單膝跪於山丘擲出毒鏢。重傷的勒烏化為橡樹上的雄鷹，腐肉片片剝落，直到吉威恩循豬蹤尋得並令其復形。勒烏懷憤擲出的長矛穿透格羅努及其身前的巨石——那塊石頭至今仍留在阿杜德威。

sensitivity.note: The paradoxical death-conditions (the spear of a year's forging, Sabbath-only) and the wounded-god-in-the-tree (Lleu as eagle in the oak, flesh rotting) are the Welsh Lugus-myth core — the closest British analogue to Balor's eye and the mistletoe of the oak; the spear through the stone is the corpus's standing-stone death (cf. Gronw's kinsman motif). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: "What means of death hast thou?" said Blodeuwedd. "That I will tell thee," said Lleu; "it is only by a manner of death that I can be slain: it is not easy to accomplish... I can only be slain by a spear, and it were a year in the making, and it were made only during the time of religious service on Sundays; and I cannot be slain within a house, nor in a tent; and if I be slain while I am standing with one foot upon a cauldron, and the other upon a buck-goat, and if I be killed beneath the canopy of a cauldron..." And Gronw rose up from the bill which is called Bryn Kyvergyr, and he rested on one knee, and flung the poisoned dart and struck him on the side, so that the shaft started out, but the head of the dart remained in his body; and Lleu rose up in the shape of an eagle, and flew away, and gave a horrible scream.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.

passages.text: And they came to that part of the country where they saw the oak, and they looked what it might be that the swine was feeding on... And Gwydion came under the tree, and looked what it might be that the eagle was. And he saw that he was an eagle, and the eagle was very wretched... And he sang an englyn, and the eagle came down to the lowest branch of the tree, and he sang another englyn, and the eagle came down to the third branch... until he came to the ground. And Gwydion struck him with his wand, and changed him into his own form... And Lleu rose up where he had rested on one foot and flung the spear at Gronw, and it pierced him through the stone that he held before him, and Gronw fell dead. And the stone that was pierced is yet to be seen, and it is called Llech Gronw.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.
